entries.title: The Ghost of the Mountains by Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi review – the secrets of the snow leopard

entries.content:
When bored, try the following game – I call it “Purr or Roar?”. Take any feline and guess whether it can purr or roar (it cannot do both because purring and roaring require different anatomical structures). Some candidates are easy: any child knows that lions and tigers roar and that a tabby does not. But between the great cats and our pets are numerous other species, from lynxes to panthers, whose anatomy is not so easy to infer. A leopard, for instance? Roar (or growl). The discreet, mountain-dwelling snow leopard? Purr.

The snow leopard is the protagonist of Kulbhushansingh Suryawanshi’s first book, a compelling and intimate look at this elusive mountain specialist. An Indian conservationist and mountaineer, Suryawanshi pursues the creature through the Himalayas and Gobi desert. This is a gritty and detailed portrait of an often misunderstood and endangered species in an increasingly hostile, crowded and hot environment.

Suryawanshi grew up in Aurangabad in the Deccan Peninsula – far away from the snow leopard’s habitat – and decided to pursue ecology after reading biologist George Schaller’s The Year of the Gorilla in the city’s public library. He writes of his admiration for western conservationists, mountaineers and explorers – Schaller, Reinhold Messner, and British imperial adventurer Francis Younghusband – and yet he is an Indian writer, writing about the ecology of his own country. As much as his book is about snow leopards, it also asks us to consider their biographers: who is it who gets to tell the story of the nonhuman lives around us?

Despite its name, the snow leopard has little in common with the leopard (its closest living relative is the tiger). And, unlike the leopard, it is adapted to the harsh and rugged terrain of the highest ranges, from India to Russia. It has an absurdly bushy tail, used both as extra limb and voluminous shawl, and large paws which act like snow shoes. What it lacks in power (it does not have a particularly strong bite), it makes up for in agility and guile (snow leopards can chase their prey down steep cliff faces; and have been known to drive horses into deep snow where they can be picked off). They are extremely difficult to spot; Suryawanshi observes that their “ochre-and-dust-colour coat with its irregular rosettes looks exactly like a rock covered with lichens”. Indeed, he muses, they should really be called “rock leopards”.

I have read much about the snow leopard, or rather books by writers searching for some ideal version of them. Suryawanshi’s book is very different, and can almost be read in opposition to the quest narratives of, say, Peter Matthiessen or Sylvain Tesson. Much like a conservationist’s diary, his book is shorn of romance, and recounts the grind of observing and counting snow leopards in remote parts of the world, far away from his wife and young daughter. He wades through snow, sets up camera traps, and tries to defuse tensions with local herders. His snow leopards are part of an ecosystem, just like any other animal; they are hated and loved, as well as being objects of indifference.

According to Suryawanshi, although snow leopards prefer to hunt wild animals, up to 70% of their diet is livestock, a recipe for conflict with local people. He talks to one herder in the Spiti Valley of the Indian Himalayas who nonchalantly relates that he shot a snow leopard after it attacked his goats, and dumped its corpse in a river. Here is no sacred object of veneration, then, but a potential pest, the equivalent of European fox (other locals speak of their fondness for the cats: a community in the village of Kibber ended up adopting and feeding a sick snow leopard, even naming him Rancho after a character in a Bollywood film).

Much of Suryawanshi’s work is dedicated to mediating conflict between the cats and locals. He assists in the design of a livestock enclosure that can deter the claws and ingenuity of a hungry snow leopard; and makes recommendations on schemes to compensate herders whose animals have been killed. Interestingly, he notes that women are the most hostile to snow leopards as they are the ones who look after livestock (and do not necessarily benefit from compensation schemes). One local woman asks: “why don’t you marry one of your snow leopards?”

The most painful section in the book relates to the bitter dispute regarding the The International Union for Conservation of Nature’s 2017 decision to downgrade the animal’s from “endangered” to “vulnerable”. Suryawanshi and his colleagues at the Snow Leopard Trust bitterly opposed the move, arguing that the decision was based on flawed science and driven by the political considerations of large NGOs in the west. In his eyes, “racial power dynamics and colonial legacies of conservation and research” were at play. As of today, the snow leopard is still classed as vulnerable.

There is a critique here of the stories that we have told ourselves about the snow leopard, an attempt to wrest it back from literary and metropolitan writers. In one section, Suryawanshi retraces Matthiessen’s steps in Nepal, but it seems as though his heart isn’t really in it. Along the way, he notices the effects of mass tourism, and learns that Nepal’s richest man, who owns an instant noodle company, had sought to build a resort in a remote village for tourists hoping to spot snow leopards. He takes a gentle swipe at Matthiessen: did the American writer ever stop to think about the consequences of mythologising the creature?

I think it’s a push to blame Matthiessen for the plight of the snow leopard, in the same way that Melville shouldn’t be held accountable for the decline in sperm whales. But Suryawanshi’s point is that stories matter: the snow leopard has become a commodity in the way that Everest has, a mountain to be summited. The effect of this book is a gradual stripping away of mystification, revealing the snow leopard to be fragile and beautiful just like any other inhabitant of high mountain ranges – the pika, the wild yak, the Pallas’s cat – but no less wondrous for it, and no less deserving of our attention and respect.

entries.title: A Sense of Occasion by Brodie Crellin review – a surprising and darkly funny debut
entries.summary: A dysfunctional family comes together for a funeral in this heartfelt, keenly observed novel Most of us come upon our family’s dysfunctions gradually, like a door that opens a little wider each year. This uncle, you find out, has had an affair; grandma has a hoarding problem. The cremation of the nuclear family illusion is a cornerstone of literature, especially when it’s hastened by one of those
entries.content:
Most of us come upon our family’s dysfunctions gradually, like a door that opens a little wider each year. This uncle, you find out, has had an affair; grandma has a hoarding problem. The cremation of the nuclear family illusion is a cornerstone of literature, especially when it’s hastened by one of those unavoidable core gatherings: weddings, births, funerals. But what happens when there was never any illusion to start with; when the story begins in the ashes?

The delight of Brodie Crellin’s accomplished, surprising debut lies in the way it wrestles with this question, and in its depiction of a family that fails to meet any conventional definition of the word. With a cutting eye and wry humour, Crellin finds fantastic power in the story of three maladjusted people reeling in the face of death, whose relationships to one another are endlessly confronting and complex.

There is friendless Patch, riddled with anxiety, who bursts into tears at the memory of the postman’s suicide and falls victim to a terrible haircut. There is Patch’s father, Robin, who is “gay, yes, mostly, but mutable”. And there is Jude, her domineering, malevolently competent cousin, a playwright who “loves to make an entrance”. They’re bound by the newly deceased Mary: Robin’s ex, Patch’s mother, and Jude’s aunt – a woman who “[didn’t] have a problem with gay men” but was lukewarm on lesbians. Orbiting this “isosceles”, as Jude calls it, is Juliette, Jude’s gleefully moneyed mother, and Mel, Mary’s neighbour. Various other characters swing in and out, all fully realised no matter how brief their appearances, my favourite of which was Mary’s poor, forgotten “empath” labrador, Leonard.

The stage is set, as Jude cruises in from Naples, for a fraught collision of past and present. As the funeral draws closer and tensions simmer, Crellin juggles the minutiae of death – chopping vegetables, arranging memorial photos – with fragmented recollections of messy family history. It’s rare to read a novel that can skip in and out of so many points of view and keep the different styles of narration intact. Yet even with regular flashbacks, A Sense of Occasion feels remarkably natural thanks to Crellin’s light touch, especially in the arch, zippy dialogue. There are shades of classic mid-century stories, particularly Dorothy Baker’s Cassandra at the Wedding, and some of the caustic social wit of Edward St Aubyn’s Melrose chronicles, but the boldness feels entirely modern.

It’s a joy, too, to read fiction that understands sex so well, and is neither sentimental nor sleazy. Crellin conveys the importance of sex as a vehicle for each character’s foibles and desires; as a shadowy place where so much can be manipulated and communicated. The book summons up a kaleidoscope of erotic experience across the spectrum, sometimes hot and sometimes ridiculous, including a quasi-incestuous relationship rendered with nuance and consideration.

If the novel leans a little hard on Jude and her mother, Juliette, for its class critiques, it’s easily forgiven on account of just how much fun it is to watch these characters crash into each other, and for the deftly nasty one-liners that they toss out. “Patch lacked the confidence conferred by a private education,” Jude thinks smugly. “But she could also say that Patch was simply less intelligent.” And yet the story never veers into mean-spirited satire, largely thanks to Patch herself, the grief-stricken daughter, who is the heartbeat of the novel. Perennially misunderstood and underestimated – including by her own mother, when she was alive – Patch is awkward but raw, a keen observer of herself and others.

There is immense pleasure and vitality – and ultimately a great deal of tenderness – in A Sense of Occasion’s depiction of flawed, strange people who love badly, and can’t help but get in the way of themselves over and over again. After all, as George Bernard Shaw wrote, “If you cannot get rid of the family skeleton, you may as well make it dance.”

entries.title: Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey gives UK poetry sales an epic boost
entries.summary: Poetry sales surpassed £8m in the first 30 weeks of 2026 and are expected to reach a record high this year thanks to blockbuster adaptation of Homer’s 2,700-year-old poemUK poetry sales are on course to reach a record high this year, buoyed by the success of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of Homer’s The Odyssey.Poetry sales surpassed £8m during the first 30 weeks of 2026, an incre
entries.content:
UK poetry sales are on course to reach a record high this year, buoyed by the success of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster film adaptation of Homer’s The Odyssey.

Poetry sales surpassed £8m during the first 30 weeks of 2026, an increase of 13.3% on the same period last year, according to data from market researchers NielsenIQ.

The category is expected to exceed £15m in annual sales for the first time since accurate records began and could reach £17m if its current momentum continues through the autumn.

Homer’s 2,700-year-old epic poem has accounted for a significant share of this year’s growth after Nolan’s adaptation – starring Matt Damon, Tom Holland, Zendaya and Anne Hathaway – brought the ancient Greek epic to a new audience. UK print sales of The Odyssey increased by 1,400% in the four weeks to 25 July compared with the same period in 2025, after the film’s release in the middle of the month.

Editions of The Odyssey and The Iliad have generated £980,000 in poetry sales so far this year – equivalent to £1.20 of every £10 spent on poetry books in Britain.

Nolan’s adaptation stormed the global box office, taking $264m (£198m) during its opening weekend, marking the director’s best ever opening.

Homer could now challenge the record for the highest annual sales by a poet in the UK. The current benchmark was set by Canadian poet and Instagram sensation Rupi Kaur, whose books, such as 2015 hit Milk and Honey, generated £1.2m through NielsenIQ BookScan’s Total Consumer Market in 2017.

The Nolan effect is also being felt in the US. Print sales across all editions of The Odyssey are up 76% so far this year, according to Circana BookScan figures.

But the poetry boom extends well beyond ancient epic. Even when sales of The Odyssey and The Iliad are removed from this year’s and last year’s figures, the category is still up 7.2% and remains on course for its best year. The three years from 2023 to 2025 were the category’s most lucrative on record.

Much of this has been driven by more commercial, social media-friendly poets. Scottish writer Donna Ashworth remains Britain’s bestselling living poet of the decade, with her 2025 collection To the Women selling almost 34,000 copies this year. However some traditionalists have questioned whether her uplifting, aphoristic work is poetry or self-help.

“The poetry sector was already enjoying an upwards trajectory before Chris Nolan tackled The Odyssey, helped in recent years by the popularity of Instapoets, including Rupi Kaur, repositioning the poetry sector from a more academic category into a lifestyle, gift and self-development genre,” said Philip Stone at NielsenIQ.

The year’s breakout poetry bestseller is from the London-based actor and poet Lucas Jones, whose debut collection, I Still Believe in Miracles, is 2026’s bestselling poetry title by value, generating £400,000, according to the Bookseller.

Classicist Emily Wilson’s acclaimed 2017 translation has been the main beneficiary of The Odyssey’s surge in sales.

Wilson herself made headlines last week when she criticised the film, saying “it has nothing convincing to say” and that it “lacks psychological, emotional, political and ethical depth”.

In a scathing article for the London Review of Books, she wrote: “Nolan’s Odyssey lacks many of the elements that make the poem great … The writing is abysmal. None of the characters has convincing motivation for their actions or words. There are no sex scenes, and all the food looks horrible.”

She added: “I would be ashamed to have written any part of this script.”

Audiobook versions of The Odyssey have also experienced renewed interest: Stephen Fry’s reading has entered Spotify’s UK audiobook top 10, while Ian McKellen’s narration has appeared in the equivalent US chart.

entries.title: Children of the Wild by Kevin Powers review – gripping tale of a friendship forged in war
entries.summary: Written by a US army veteran, this novel of courage and cruelty during the first world war is filled with unsettlingly authoritative depictions of violence – but its characters are less believable Kevin Powers’s fourth novel marks a return to the themes and subject matter of his acclaimed debut The Yellow Birds, winner of the 2012 Guardian first book award. Through the lives of its central charact
entries.content:
Kevin Powers’s fourth novel marks a return to the themes and subject matter of his acclaimed debut The Yellow Birds, winner of the 2012 Guardian first book award. Through the lives of its central characters, it explores the courage, folly, cruelty and absurdity involved in war, and the challenges of adjusting to civilian life afterwards. But while The Yellow Birds focused on the experience of US soldiers fighting in Iraq, where Powers himself served between 2003 and 2004, Children of the Wild is set amid the carnage of the first world war.

It follows the fortunes of two young men from a remote valley in Virginia. Roy is the arrogant young heir to a wealthy local landowner; Ennis is an orphan of unknown origin who has been living, like a character in a fairytale, in a shack on the top of a mountain. Ennis and Roy are first linked in a love triangle when Ennis is lured off his mountain top by his desire for Samantha, the daughter of the local minister, whose eyes have the “lustre of smoky quartz”. Roy has expected to marry Samantha, but she chooses feral Ennis. Roy accepts the setback remarkably swiftly, transferring his affections to Esther, the wealthy and shallow sister of his college roommate, Fintan. Roy and Ennis settle their differences with a mighty punch-up that cements an unlikely friendship between them.

When Roy joins the army to fight in France as an officer, he persuades Ennis to come with him as a private. This becomes a source of guilt to Roy as the novel unfolds. Unequal in terms of class and status, Roy and Ennis are also asymmetrically talented at killing. Roy, though nominally the leader, is haunted by terrifying dreams and finds the responsibility of his role overwhelming. Ennis turns out to have an Achilles-like genius for warfare.

Born out of a brawl, the relationship between Roy and Ennis turns out to be by far the strongest attachment in the novel. It’s reinforced by subsequent acts of violence that include killings on and off the battlefield. Roy is both in awe of Ennis and fearful of him. Indifferent to praise or glory, Ennis is “at home in a dark corner of his soul that Roy didn’t even want to acknowledge existed in his own”.

Powers is a tremendously gifted writer. He has an amazing knack for storytelling that seems to unfold visually and conveys landscapes, gestures and complex military engagements with great flair. His economical prose makes brisk work of a gripping tale that includes violent set pieces on the battlefields of France, war crimes, a pandemic, a quest through the mountains of Ohio, murders, a flashback to the bloodshed at Little Big Horn, and a powerful ending that reminds you, once more, of the heartbreak war brings in its wake.

Powers writes about violence and its impact on both perpetrators and victims in a way that feels unsettlingly authoritative. When Ennis commandeers a German machine gun, you sense that the scene is informed by more than academic research: Powers was himself a machine-gunner in the Iraq war. Various characters, including a civil war veteran, punctuate self-aggrandising Roy’s delusions about warfare and loss with memorably gritty wisdom. “Every single person on this earth has a hole inside them where someone they loved used to be,” one person tells him. “You sit there thinking that hole inside of you is special.”

Buried in the pages of the book is a telling allusion that hints at Powers’s ambition for it. On two occasions, in the context of terrible acts of violence – a scalping and a lynching – different characters utter these words to Roy: “Come and see.” Both times, Roy draws our attention to the phrase by repeating it: “‘Come and see’? It was familiar, but Roy couldn’t place it.”

Powers wants the reader to notice the words and supply the missing context: “Come and see” is the dark invitation that John the Revelator receives in the final book of the Bible to witness the apocalypse. It’s also the title of a Soviet film directed by Elem Klimov that has a strong claim to be the most harrowing war movie ever made. Very much like Klimov’s film, Powers mixes incredible visual intensity with the mythic and surreal in order to illuminate the apocalyptic extremes of human behaviour.

Yet his desire to make the story resonate at an epic level also makes parts of the novel melodramatic and implausible. When you notice the characters are mythic archetypes – Roy Young, Ennis Duke, the flawed Arthurian king and the Lancelot who steals his Guinevere – they seem a little less real as people. Ennis’s journey down the mountain and his progression from feral cow-wrangler to cold-eyed killer never feels fully persuasive and is punctuated by moments of improbability. This isn’t limited to Ennis: characters have a habit of doing things that are dramatically striking, but psychologically far-fetched. Samantha distributes presents to the local children with the corpse of her dead father in the wagon. Roy heads off to the Bighorn Mountains for a mission that’s supposed to be heartfelt, but feels like hollow spectacle. Ennis returns from the war and perpetrates a bizarre and self-sabotaging act of violence. And then there’s Fintan Thoreau, Roy’s ghastly future brother-in-law, whose villainy motivates an important section of the plot but feels cartoonish.

There’s also something uncomfortable about the book’s representation of violence. Officially, violence is repellent, but it’s pretty cool too, especially when our heroes are cutting a swathe through German soldiers, who are depicted with a one-sidedness that reminded me of the jingoistic Warlord comics that were a guilty pleasure of my childhood. At one point, Roy is struggling to find the cold-heartedness to dispatch a German soldier who is pleading for his life. Roy looks over at Ennis, with a look “that begged him for permission to be free of this man’s death”. The permission is supplied by the author: the two-faced Boche sneakily pulls out a knife thus making him utterly unworthy to live.

Though I enjoyed the book a great deal and admired Powers’s bravura, economical prose, I ended up comparing it to other books about the same conflict. The first world war has many chronicles: All Quiet on the Western Front, Good-Bye to All That, Birdsong, Pat Barker’s Regeneration trilogy. The best of these manage to depict the awfulness of warfare with both more banality and more humour. I recently reread Frederick Manning’s 1929 novel The Middle Parts of Fortune alongside Alice Winn’s 2023 debut In Memoriam. I found their foul-mouthed soldiers and doomed public schoolboys more lastingly real than the avatars of Children of the Wild, with their murky backstories and portentous dream lives.

entries.title: Geography of Heaven by Rory MacLean – soul-searching journeys into the afterlife
entries.summary: From an ashram in India to an ayahuasca ceremony in Peru, a travel writer searches for meaning after the death of his wifeIn this moving, sometimes grandiloquent grief-memoir-cum-travelogue, Rory MacLean pairs an affinity for new-age thinking with a habit of loftily holding forth (“none of us are created for naught”, “love can but lead to truth”) and a proclivity for arresting one-liners (“I watch
entries.content:
In this moving, sometimes grandiloquent grief-memoir-cum-travelogue, Rory MacLean pairs an affinity for new-age thinking with a habit of loftily holding forth (“none of us are created for naught”, “love can but lead to truth”) and a proclivity for arresting one-liners (“I watched gods walk on fire”). In his search for meaning in the five years after his wife’s untimely death from cancer, he shows himself to be both refreshingly broad-minded and unnecessarily crotchety, like a more cantankerous Michael Palin.

MacLean’s work as a travel writer has taken him across the world, whether flying a handbuilt plane over Crete or riding shotgun with a drug warlord in Burma. This is his first book since losing Katrin, for 32 years the “fixed point” in his life, whose final weeks and moments he describes tenderly. Unable to process her death, he turns to travel to seek out “thin places”: áiteanna tanaí in Celtic mythology, where the veil between worlds is porous. Starting in Jerusalem, his quest takes him to more than a dozen sacred locations, including an ashram in India, a Native American community in South Dakota, an “excruciating” Vipassanā retreat in Suffolk and, inevitably, an ayahuasca ceremony in Peru.

You can’t fault his commitment. He takes the alarming decision – mere weeks before the 7 October attacks – to infiltrate an Israeli settlement in the West Bank, hiding in the shadows from IDF patrols, in an attempt to recreate the circumstances under which Jacob (“a traveller like me”) dreamed of a ladder to heaven. In the US, he faces an oncoming tornado, “too transfixed by the unfolding storm” to seek shelter; in Bhutan, he spends two days travelling to a Buddhist festival along a road that is “little more than a narrow ledge hacked into the rock face”.

MacLean’s skills as a travel writer are evident. He brings to life a Herzogian boat journey down a river into the Amazon, “twisting like a serpent towards another world”. He describes a cremation ground in Bhutan in rich, resonant detail, from the “barley burned in a metal basin, its smell said to keep hungry ghosts at bay”, to the throaty chanting of the monks. In South Africa, he consults a sangoma or diviner; to this day, the country has four times more traditional diviners and herbalists than medical doctors. At the Rosebud Sioux Reservation, he witnesses a remarkable ritual involving trance-like dancing and offerings of flesh. The discussions of Victorian spiritualism and the use of AI to bypass grief are thoughtful and well judged.

But there are jarring tonal shifts, from the pompous (“Does sanctity fall from above or is it conditional on social convention, I wondered?”) to the colloquial (“kick the bucket”, “bunkum”). And more than once, the book is let down by outdated language about minority groups (described as “crippled” and “swarthy-skinned”). Do we really need to know whether every woman he encounters is “slender” or “chubby”?

Throughout, MacLean treads the line between credulous and open-minded. Science is invoked occasionally, only to be dismissed as “reductionist” and “pathetic”. Instead, he becomes fixated on numerology, calculating “the maths” of when Katrin will be reincarnated (according to different people he consults, 49 days after her death, or years later, potentially as a dog). He compiles a dossier of evidence that, in his mind, proves “without doubt” that Katrin’s soul lives on: a dream, a sunbeam, a blue ribbon, a friend’s furniture in Mexico being inexplicably rearranged.

In each new location, his soul-searching follows a pattern: initial disappointment, followed by a last-minute breakthrough. Much of the book hinges on him feeling a vague, indefinable presence – a tingling, a shift in the air – undoubtedly profound to him but almost impossible to put into words (“something infinitely subtle … it was there, and more than nothing”), which can be frustrating for the reader. A somewhat belaboured flight metaphor eventually leads him, many figurative and literal air miles later, to the realisation that what matters is the journey, not the destination.

entries.title: The August Coup by Robert Service review – the drink-soaked collapse of the Soviet Union
entries.summary: This brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifullyMarxist-Leninist rule in Russia lasted 74 years, and in August 1991 it effectively collapsed in just three days: clear evidence of how hollowed out it had become. In the period that followed, Russia tried parliamentary democracy and unalloyed capitalism, then sank back into auto
entries.content:
Marxist-Leninist rule in Russia lasted 74 years, and in August 1991 it effectively collapsed in just three days: clear evidence of how hollowed out it had become. In the period that followed, Russia tried parliamentary democracy and unalloyed capitalism, then sank back into autocracy. Now it’s struggling under a wholly unnecessary war against its neighbour and former possession, Ukraine.

Why did the system of Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev and Brezhnev vanish so fast, without a fight? Because that’s how regimes fall in Russia: look at tsarism in 1917. (It almost happened again in June 2023, when the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin’s men marched on Moscow largely unopposed; Vladimir Putin might have gone the way of Nicholas II had he not made some pretty wholesale promises to Prigozhin, then allegedly blown him up two months later.)

Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985 with the intention of saving the USSR. Instead, he oversaw its death. He was a charming, decent man but no visionary, and the two medicines he brought to the patient’s bedside, perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), proved to be wholly ineffective. The brief coup of August 1991 against him, headed by Vladimir Kryuchkov, the boss of the KGB, was the kneejerk response of a bureaucracy that knew things were going wrong but had absolutely no idea what to do about it. It failed quickly, and Gorbachev was back at his desk within days, but the coup had damaged him fatally. Four months later, at the end of 1991, he was bundled out of power by the tough, brutal, boozy muzhik, Boris Yeltsin.

Robert Service, author of The August Coup, is the English-speaking world’s foremost historian of 20th-century Russia and Bolshevism. His biographies of the three major Soviet leaders, Lenin, Stalin and Trotsky, are outstanding, even in that crowded field. In writing about the death of the system that these prodigies and monsters helped to create, Service has displayed a remarkable grasp of the vast sources, and a delightfully clear writing style which makes even the complexities of Soviet bureaucracy easy to understand. Compared with his earlier subjects, the story of the coup against Gorbachev and the collapse of the USSR is moderately simple; but Service guides the reader through the chaos of the collapsing system and the machinations of the coup leaders with ease and grace.

After the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and the loss of the various Soviet satrapies in eastern and central Europe, the USSR was falling apart, and Gorbachev, as its president, was shedding power and influence. No one knew how many Soviet republics would break away, and Gorbachev’s plan for running the rump of the union was bitterly contested. Yeltsin was the president of the Russian Republic, the largest, richest and most effective part of the old USSR. The two men were in angry contention. The coup leaders didn’t support either of them: they wanted to go back to a system which would restore as much Soviet power as possible. The assumption at the time was that the KGB had led the coup to protect its own interests, but Service demonstrates that Kryuchkov, the KGB boss, was much more concerned about the overall collapse of the Soviet system. And anyway, many KGB officers refused to join the coup.

I was lucky enough to be in Moscow during those extraordinary days. Service captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully. The coup leaders lost their faith in what they were doing almost immediately, and many of them didn’t have much to begin with. They argued, betrayed each other, or were paralysed by fear or torpor. Most of the people involved left some account of what happened, so the records available to Service were particularly rich. He provides us with a graphic description of the fatal press conference that the plotters gave at 5pm on the first day of the coup. The acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire day and his hands were visibly shaking. The press conference was broadcast live on state television, so everyone could see the condition he was in. After that, failure was certain.

The basic reason it collapsed, though, was that the plotters didn’t manage to get hold of Yeltsin. It was easy enough to imprison Gorbachev at his palatial residence, Zarya, on the Crimean coast, where he was holidaying with his wife Raisa and their daughter; but Yeltsin remained free, and had use of the Russian republic’s Moscow headquarters, known as the White House. You might expect communist plotters to be good at cutting communications and taking over the media, but no one stopped Yeltsin from phoning allies and friends around Russia and across the world. Nor did they try to prevent him making his famous speech from a tank in front of the White House, condemning the coup and pledging to support democracy. It was a good speech, and the television coverage of it was seen worldwide. Again, no one pulled the plugs. Journalists like me were able to broadcast live throughout the coup. Yeltsin stayed inside the White House, mostly protected by a small crowd of unarmed demonstrators whose numbers dropped as the first night wore on and the rain came down.

Yet Yeltsin suffered from the same weaknesses as many of the plotters. In the lobby of the White House I begged to be allowed to go up to his office and interview him, but was told he was too busy speaking to world leaders and organising the opposition. Later, the former Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze arrived to see him. When he came out of the building an hour afterwards, he announced that Yeltsin had told him he would defend Russia’s freedom to the last drop of blood in his body. Stirring stuff. Three years later I reminisced with Shevardnadze about it all. He laughed. “When I got into Yeltsin’s office, he was lying unconscious on the floor with a couple of empty vodka bottles beside him.” But what about him fighting to his last drop of blood? “What do you think would have happened if I’d come out and told you I couldn’t speak to Yeltsin because he was dead drunk?”

Such was the chaos and absurdity surrounding the death of the Soviet Union. In the days that followed no one had any idea where authority lay. The famously brave and entrepreneurial cameraman Rory Peck and I marched into KGB headquarters, the Lubyanka, and filmed in Kryuchkov’s own office. After that we even filmed among the ultra-secret KGB files. The next day Rory offered to buy the contents of the Central Museum of the Revolution for a million dollars. Only the fact that the official in charge couldn’t find a bank prepared to accept that much cash stopped the deal going through. We tend to forget the details of this pivotal episode. Perhaps Russia’s troubled history since 1991 has wiped them from our memories. Now Service has brought his magnificent grasp of Soviet history to the task of chronicling the ludicrous way it ended: not with a bang, but with the clink of vodka bottles.

entries.title: Exhibition by Alex Hyde review – an elegiac love letter to the YBA era
entries.summary: London’s 90s art scene forms the backdrop to this tale of a complex relationship between two artists whose identities become entangled in their creative collaborationFor all the wrong reasons, Damien Hirst’s Shark (The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living) has a claim to being the most prescient British artwork of the last half-century: a grim parable of neoliberalism. In
entries.content:
For all the wrong reasons, Damien Hirst’s Shark (The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living) has a claim to being the most prescient British artwork of the last half-century: a grim parable of neoliberalism. In 1991, it was still possible to mistake the predatory violence of that system for a kind of animal vitality. But today, open-mouthed, dead-eyed and decayed, it speaks only of a regime preserved far beyond its natural lifespan, lauded exclusively by institutions that can profit from its ugliness.

Alex Hyde’s second novel, an elegant Künstlerroman which plays out during a lightly fictionalised version of the YBA explosion, explores the resonance of that particular cultural inflection point: a moment when the collapse of the postwar cultural settlement, municipal culture and public institutions was transfigured decisively and ubiquitously into individualised, confessional artistic capital.

It tells the story of Rabble Stone, a working-class photography student who moves to London and falls into the orbit of a moneyed, cosmopolitan artistic set who are alternately impressed, baffled and alienated by the seriousness of both her manner and her work. Among them is the unnamed artist, now deceased, to whom the novel is primarily addressed through a series of elegiac reminiscences, unpicking their entanglement as friends, muses and occasional antagonists.

Central to this relationship are the ways in which their respective selfhoods become intertwined and distorted via their ongoing artistic collaboration. Rabble begins to photograph the artist, a series of intimate, confrontational portraits that are eventually physically incorporated into the artist’s figurative drawings and paintings. Hyde’s descriptions of the work strongly evoke Tracey Emin, as does its subsequent journey from localised art-world curio to highly valuable, globally exhibited market commodity.

Thematically, there is an air of predictability in how this all plays out. Questions of self-authorship, doubling, co-option, plagiarism and the quasi-erotics of display and representation are handled well enough, but will feel overfamiliar to many readers. There are also occasions where the language is imprecise and hesitant in ways that appear to be stylistic lapses rather than stylistic choices. Hyde leans heavily on superposition; needs are “base and noble at the same time”, faces are “ugly and beautiful at the same time”, characters feel “something and nothing at the same time”. And just as frequently, the prose lapses into a hazy self-correction that reads less as an evocation of the unreliability of memory and more as syntactic hesitance.

The novel also contains passages of precise and inventive writing. Hyde is especially admirable on a rhythmic level, demonstrating comfort with the staccato and fragmentary as well as the more languid and expansive descriptive work she uses sparingly but to great effect. She writes particularly well and tenderly about bodily exhaustion, both among the working-class communities of Rabble’s youth, and the struggling artists she later encounters in New York, both made brittle by virtue of their position in the economic value chain. Similarly, the character of Duncan, an effervescent aesthete who succumbs to the ravages of addiction, is handled with delicacy, a lightness of touch that captures the horror of chasing ghosts until you finally become one.

Also commendable is Hyde’s willingness to grapple with the issue that plagues ekphrastic writing in practically all of its forms. To write about images is to render things that are fundamentally spatial, relational and simultaneous into sentences that are necessarily sequential, disaggregated and hierarchical. The standard way out of this dilemma for a novelist is to focus the description such that it tells us less about the artwork than about the sensibilities and feelings of the character viewing it. In Exhibition, however, Hyde repeatedly goes a step further and engages directly with the theoretical challenge at hand, allowing Rabble to talk at length about composition, the role of the lens, the function of framing; how photographs “are not taken … they are made”.

And that Rabble is a photographer, rather than, say, a sculptor or a painter, hints at what appears to me to be the novel’s central philosophical concern; namely remembrance, nostalgia and preservation. It is photographs we turn to, after all, to re-narrativise our lives, to reflect on distances travelled and the alternate turns we might have taken along the way. That feeling of melancholic reflection, of abundant futures concertinaed into the inevitability of the present, suffuses Exhibition and is its primary achievement. For just as Rabble is left mourning lost friends and collaborators, we as readers are left mourning the loss of something larger and more significant, an entire structure of possibility. Exhibition is a eulogy for a world of livable rents, radical art schools, free higher education and opportunities for working-class artists, for a society in which a life like Rabble’s, spent making beautiful things out of the people and places she loved, was not seen as a risible pipe dream or as the gate-kept preserve of the select few.

Keiran Goddard’s latest novel is I See Buildings Fall Like Lightning (Abacus). Exhibition by Alex Hyde is published by Granta (£14.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com

entries.title: What we’re reading: writers and readers on the books they enjoyed in July
entries.summary: Max Porter, Daisy Johnson, Avni Doshi and Guardian readers discuss the titles they have read over the last month. entries.content:
Max Porter, writer

I recently read Gaining Ground by Joan Barfoot. It’s one of the best novels I’ve ever read about what it means to live with others, or decide not to; what we owe the people we love, the natural world, and ourselves. I also really enjoyed Robert Frost, by Robert Frost and Stacy Skolnik. It’s not that Robert Frost; it’s an itinerant young American Robert Frost who jots down his thoughts and observations on homelessness, food, value, music, drugs, the philosophical wastelands of contemporary life, and Stacy Skolnik has turned them into these delightful, oddly profound, poems. Also, coming soon, End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. Everyone should read it. It tells us exactly what’s going on.

Max Porter is the author of books including Shy and Grief Is the Thing With Feathers

Richard, Guardian reader

I am reading Headlights by the American horror writer CJ Leede. This is her third novel. I think she has the potential to be the 21st century’s Stephen King – she’s that good! Headlights is a pitch-black horror novel with overtones of Silence of the Lambs and Osgood Perkins’ fabulous film Longlegs. It is also a love letter to King’s The Shining and has a strong environmental message too, concerning man’s uneasy and destructive relationship with the natural world. Leede is such a wonderful writer of prose. Her characters are three-dimensional and you care about them almost immediately (which makes what she does to some of them all the more horrible!). She has an obvious love of the American landscape and describes it beautifully, and the book’s relationship with The Shining will have horror lovers squealing with delight – there are little Easter eggs peppered throughout the book.

Daisy Johnson, writer

Lately I am to be found loudly and excitedly recommending The Corner That Held Them by Sylvia Townsend Warner, first published in 1948. Set over 200 years and taking in the Black Death, the Great Revolt of 1381 and much bickering, the novel follows a convent of nuns living in the British Fenlands. I’ve also loved reading The Empusium, an equally claustrophobic book by Olga Tokarczuk which, thrillingly, is described as “a health resort horror story” on the cover. It follows a young man with failing health who visits a sanatorium in the mountains to recover. It is a rather glorious and surreal romp.

Long Wave by Daisy Johnson is published by Jonathan Cape (£18.99). To support the Guardian buy a copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply

Sarah, Guardian reader

This month (perhaps not so subconsciously) I seem to have been drawn mostly to both fiction and nonfiction featuring women facing personal challenges. In fiction, Tamarin by Priya Hein and Under Water by Tara Menon have been favourites this month, and I think the books pair well together: both feature women who return to their homeland after life-changing experiences. In nonfiction, My Cantopop Nights by Emma-Lee Moss was a thoroughly enjoyable read about one woman’s search to find home and her identity in Hong Kong. Her experiences of motherhood resonated with me, and I was transported back to my own time spent in Hong Kong a decade ago. Finally, a hybrid of the two genres: Said the Dead by Doireann Ní Ghríofa. I devoured this book, which vividly brings to life the stories of a number of women who inhabited a psychiatric hospital in Ireland in the 1890s and early 20th century, the result of obsessive research by the author.

Avni Doshi, writer

While researching for my next novel, in which one of the characters is an artist, I came across a brilliant book called Colour by Victoria Finlay. Finlay dives deep into the fascinating history of where colour comes from. It reads like an adventure into the painter’s palette. Expect intrigue, beetles and dead bodies. Andrea Bajani’s The Anniversary was also a recent favourite. The story follows a grown man unpicking the web of his painful childhood. A slim book written in crisp prose, there isn’t a word out of place. I read it in one sitting. I also loved and have been widely recommending A Splintering by Dur e Aziz Amna, in which a cunning and ambitious woman from a village in Pakistan reshapes the future that was set for her. Rarely have I read a character so ruthless and irresistible. Her hunger growls on the page.
